Mughira asked most about the Dajjal; the Prophet called him 'my son', said the Dajjal would not harm him and is more insignificant to Allah than his rivers and bread.
Abu Musa left Umar's door after asking permission three times unanswered, as the Prophet taught; Umar demanded a witness, and Abu Sa'id, the youngest present, testified for him.
Permission is sought three times, then one goes back; Umar demanded a witness from Abu Musa, and Abu Sa'id and Ubayy ibn Ka'b confirmed the Prophet said it.
When Jabir sought permission and answered the Prophet's question of who it was with 'It is I', the Prophet came out repeating 'It is I' as if disapproving.
Permission guards against glances; the Prophet said he would have pierced the eye of a man peeping through his door, and a household may put out an uninvited peeper's eyes.
Jarir asked the Prophet about a sudden glance, and he commanded him to turn his eyes away.
The rider greets the walker, the walker greets the one seated, and the small group greets the larger.
The Prophet told people to avoid sitting on the paths or else give them their rights: lowering the gaze, causing no harm, returning greetings, good talk, commanding good, forbidding evil.
A Muslim owes his brother five or six rights: returning his greeting, accepting his invitation, giving advice when asked, answering his sneeze, visiting him when ill and following his bier.
The People of the Book are answered 'And upon you', since some Jews greeted with 'Death be upon you'; when Aisha cursed them back, the Prophet said Allah loves kindness.
The Prophet said not to greet the Jews and Christians first, and when meeting one of them on the road, to force him to its narrowest part.
The Prophet greeted the boys he passed, and Anas and Thabit after him did the same.
The Prophet told Ibn Mas'ud that a raised curtain, or hearing his quiet talk, was the sign he could come in until told otherwise.
Umar called out to the tall Sauda when the Prophet's wives went out for their needs; revelation followed, in one report permitting them out, in another the veil verses.
No man may stay the night with a married woman but her husband or mahram, the husband's brother is like death, and none should enter an absent man's house alone.
Seen with a wife, once Safiyya visiting his i'tikaf, the Prophet told passers-by who she was, as Satan circulates in man like blood and might put evil in their hearts.
Of three men reaching the Prophet's circle, one took a gap and Allah sheltered him, one sat behind from shyness, and one left, so Allah turned away from him.
No one may make another rise to take his seat, even on Friday, but should say 'make room'; one who leaves his place and returns has most right to it.
A eunuch who visited the Prophet's household described a woman's body, so the Prophet said such men should not enter upon the women, who then veiled themselves from him.
Asma bint Abu Bakr did the work of Zubair's house and horse until given a servant, and felt shy, recalling Zubair's jealousy, when the Prophet offered her a ride.
When three are together, two should not converse secretly apart from the third until others join, for it grieves him.
Gabriel recited protection over the ill Prophet from envy and the evil eye, which the Prophet said is real, telling anyone asked to bathe for it to bathe.
Labid ibn al-A'sam of Banu Zuraiq cast a spell on the Prophet; answering his supplication, Allah informed him through two men that it lay in a well and cured him.
A Jewish woman brought the Prophet poisoned meat to kill him; he ate some, told her Allah would never let her, and refused his Companions' request to kill her.
The Prophet supplicated over the sick, rubbing them with his right hand and blowing the Mu'awwidhatan over them, and Aisha did so for him in his last illness.
The Prophet permitted incantation against poison, scorpion stings, pustules and the evil eye, and used dust and saliva, with Allah's name, as a cure.
Having forbidden incantation, the Prophet allowed it against snake and scorpion poison and the evil eye once he heard the words, saying there is no harm in incantation without polytheism.
A Companion cured a scorpion-stung tribal chief by reciting al-Fatiha and was given sheep; the Prophet asked how he knew it was an incantation and asked for a share.
For bodily pain the Prophet taught saying Bismillah thrice and seeking refuge in Allah's power seven times, and for the devil Khinzab confusing prayer, seeking refuge and spitting left thrice.

Every disease has a remedy by Allah's permission; the Prophet named cupping, honey and cauterisation though disliking cautery himself, cauterised wounded Companions, and was cupped and paid the cupper.
Fever comes from the raging heat of Hell, so cool it with water, as Asma did by sprinkling water at a feverish woman's collar.
In his illness the Prophet gestured against medicine poured into his mouth, and on recovering ordered it poured into the mouths of all except Ibn Abbas, who had been absent.
The Prophet told Umm Qais not to press her infant's uvula but use Indian aloeswood, which holds seven remedies including one for pleurisy, and sprinkled water on the boy's urine.
Nigella seed is a remedy for every disease except death, talbina comforts a grieving heart, and honey, given repeatedly, cured a man's loose bowels, for Allah spoke the truth.
Plague is a calamity sent on the Children of Israel or earlier peoples; do not enter a land where it breaks out, nor flee one where you are.
At Sargh, told of plague in Syria, Umar consulted the emigrants, Ansar and Quraysh elders and turned back, from Divine Decree to Divine Decree, as Abd al-Rahman's report confirmed.
The Prophet denied transitive disease, evil omens, safar, hama and ghoul, asking who infected the first camel, and also said the sick should not be brought to the healthy.
There is no transitive disease and no divination, but the Prophet liked the good omen, which is a good word that one hears.
If bad luck exists in anything, the Prophet said, it is in the house, the woman and the horse, or in one report the land, the servant and the horse.
Asked about pre-Islamic practices, the Prophet forbade visiting soothsayers, said omens should not hold one back, and allowed line-drawing only if it matches that of a prophet who drew lines.
